title: Min–max principles for singular values
subtitle: G2 lecture 052000 · expanded mathematical companion
adaptation: Standalone companion adapted from the source spoken lecture and display-only mathematics appendix. Explicit hypotheses, stepwise proofs, worked examples, and local vector diagrams; no narration edits.

slides.title: Singular values as optimization problems
slides.lead: For a rectangular map A:E→F, singular values measure how strongly A stretches optimally chosen source directions.
body: The singular-value decomposition gives right singular vectors v₁,…,vₙ with descending singular values σ₁≥⋯≥σₙ≥0. Along v_i, the output length is exactly σ_i.
The min–max principle recovers σ_j without relying on any specific basis: one player removes strong directions and another looks for the largest remaining output.
slides.takeaway: Singular values are intrinsic answers to geometric subspace games.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 052000 · Singular values as optimization problems

slides.title: Start from the positive Gram operator
slides.lead: The source Gram operator A*A is positive, and its eigenvalues are the squared singular values.
body: Let A*A v_i=σ_i² v_i in an orthonormal basis, ordered with σ₁≥σ₂≥⋯. For any x=∑c_i v_i, the squared output norm is ∑σ_i²|c_i|².
This identity reduces the variational arguments to selecting source directions while controlling a weighted sum of squared coordinates.
slides.takeaway: Apply eigenvalue geometry to A*A and then take nonnegative square roots.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 052000 · Start from the positive Gram operator

slides.title: Remove j−1 source directions
slides.lead: An adversary first chooses a (j−1)-dimensional subspace L to discard.
body: Among unit vectors perpendicular to L, take the largest possible output length. The adversary wants this maximum as small as possible.
Discarding span(v₁,…,v_{j−1}) removes the strongest singular directions, leaving worst remaining stretch σ_j. This supplies the upper bound in the min-over-L characterization.
slides.takeaway: The optimal discarded subspace is spanned by the j−1 strongest right singular directions.

slides.title: Why no other discarded space does better
slides.lead: Every (j−1)-plane L must leave a unit vector inside the span of the first j right singular vectors.
body: Indeed that j-dimensional span and L⊥ intersect nontrivially by the dimension inequality. Every unit vector in the first j singular directions has output norm at least σ_j.
Thus the maximum stretch on L⊥ is always at least σ_j, proving the reverse inequality and completing the first min–max formula.
slides.takeaway: The dimension-intersection argument forces a strong direction to survive every deletion.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 052000 · Why no other discarded space does better

slides.title: The complementary max–min game
slides.lead: Instead choose a j-dimensional subspace W and ask for the weakest unit vector inside it.
body: Taking W=span(v₁,…,v_j) gives minimum output length σ_j. For any other j-plane, dimension counting forces an intersection with the span of v_j,…,vₙ, where every output length is at most σ_j.
Consequently no j-plane has a larger minimum, giving the second characterization.
slides.takeaway: The optimal retained j-plane is spanned by the j strongest right singular directions.

slides.title: A concrete rectangular example
body: Its source Gram operator is diag(25,4), so σ₁=5 and σ₂=2. To find σ₂, delete the strongest x-direction and maximize over its y-axis complement.
Alternatively retain the full two-dimensional source and minimize output length over unit vectors; the weakest stretch is again 2. The codomain dimension does not enter the game directly.
slides.takeaway: The variational principle works for rectangular maps and uses source dimensions.

slides.title: Connection with Courant–Fischer
slides.lead: The eigenvalue min–max principle applied to the self-adjoint Gram operator gives the singular-value version.
body: Courant–Fischer describes the jth eigenvalue of A*A by optimizing its Rayleigh quotient ⟨A*A x,x⟩ over appropriate subspaces.
But ⟨A*A x,x⟩=‖Ax‖², and the square root is monotone on nonnegative numbers. Taking square roots therefore turns the eigenvalue formula exactly into the two singular-value games.
slides.takeaway: Singular-value min–max is Courant–Fischer for the positive Gram operator.

slides.title: A rank-constrained approximation consequence
slides.lead: Suppose B has rank at most j−1 and is proposed as an approximation to A.
body: Rank–nullity guarantees dim ker B≥n−j+1. On ker B, the error (A−B)x equals Ax. The min–max principle forces some unit vector in this kernel to have ‖Ax‖≥σ_j.
Therefore no rank-(j−1) approximation can have operator-norm error below σ_j. This is the lower bound behind optimal low-rank approximation.
slides.takeaway: Low rank necessarily loses at least one direction with stretch σ_j.

slides.title: Zero singular values are part of the statement
slides.lead: If A has rank r<n, then σ_{r+1}=⋯=σₙ=0.
body: Choosing W inside ker A shows how the weak directions behave, and the min–max formulas remain valid without inventing output singular vectors for those zeros.
The source-based formulation is therefore robust for noninjective and rectangular maps. It orders all n singular values, counting the appropriate zero values.
slides.takeaway: Singular-value games naturally include kernel directions and zero singular values.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 052000 · Zero singular values are part of the statement

slides.title: Reconstruct both optimizations
slides.lead: An orthonormal singular basis and one dimension-counting argument suffice.
body: First discard the j−1 strongest right singular vectors and compute the remaining maximum. Then prove every other deletion leaves a unit vector in the top j-dimensional span.
For the dual game, keep the top j span and prove every competing j-plane intersects the bottom n−j+1 span. This gives the two formulas with no coordinate dependence in their final statements.
slides.takeaway: The two min–max proofs differ only in which intersecting subspaces the game selects.
